To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the mitotic checkpoint is essential to maintain chromosome stability during tumor cell division and that its inactivation leads to increased chromosome segregation errors and cell death in tumor cell lines.
inactivation of the checkpoint leads to increased chromosome missegregation and cell death, and that this effect is more pronounced in cancer cells than in normal cells.

inactivation of the spindle assembly checkpoint by RNAi-mediated depletion leads to a dramatic increase in chromosome missegregation, which in turn leads to an increase in cell death in tumor cell populations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of mitosis and the mitotic checkpoint.
understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying chromosome segregation in human tumor cells.
the identification of new therapeutic strategies to kill tumor cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
inactivation of the spindle assembly checkpoint can increase chromosome missegregation and cell death in tumor cell lines.
the mitotic checkpoint is a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of cancer, and that the use of small interfering RNAs is a powerful tool for the identification of such targets.
inhibition of the checkpoint can lead to aneuploidal cells, which are prone to die, and therefore inhibition of the checkpoint might be a useful anti-cancertreatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mitotic checkpoint is an important tumor defense mechanism, which can be targeted to kill cancer cells.
we have identified a new anti-cancer strategy that exploits a hallmark of cancer cells.
the mitotic checkpoint, a cell cycle checkpoint that delays mitosis until all the chromosomes are attached to the mitosis apparatus, is an essential component of the mitotic machinery.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mitotic checkpoint is an attractive anti-cancer target.
targeting the mitotic checkpoint can lead to cell death in cancer cells.
the mitotic checkpoint can be used to selectively kill cancer cells.
